title: A background-error slope cannot identify zero initialization in a 2017-2025 NHC surge audit
abstract: A published NHC surge audit linked range errors to background water and found that subtraction removed most exceedances. We test whether this identifies omission of the full background. A December 2024 NWS statement describes typical P-Surge initial water levels of 0.5-1.0 ft. In the same 795 storm-gauge units from 2017-2025, observed exceedances fall from 9.69% to 1.51% after full background subtraction. If 0.75 ft is already represented, subtraction of only the remaining anomaly leaves 8.81%. The paired storm-bootstrap 95% change interval is -2.50 to +0.93 percentage points. A uniform 0.75 ft subtraction alone leaves 1.76%. We prove that a constant initial level leaves the background-error slope unchanged when a regression has an intercept. The observed high-tide slope remains 1.079 under all tested offsets. Under a conditional 0.5-1.0 ft range for each unit, sharp exceedance bounds are 5.53-12.96%. This challenges full-background attribution, not the source counts. We do not know historical run-specific initialization, and the additive shift is not a hydrodynamic rerun. Point gauges, retrospective backgrounds and area-range matching limit inference. Code, aggregate results, an independent arithmetic check and exact provenance are included.

display.caption: Exceedance fractions change with the assumed already represented initial level. All comparisons use 795 storm-gauge units. Lines show storm-bootstrap 95% intervals. Initial levels are sensitivity assumptions, not recovered operational settings.

citations.reason: We reuse the fixed published matched table and reproduce its counts. We challenge the interpretation that these counts and a near-unit slope identify omission of the full background.
Seasonal attribution remained after gauge and storm controls. Constant-level invariance also applies to that design.
Primary documentation of typical initial water levels.
